rules.message: `.flushall(`/`.flushdb(` (or a quoted `'FLUSHALL'`/`'FLUSHDB'` command literal, e.g. `sendCommand(['FLUSHALL'])`) wipes EVERY key in the database/instance — reachable from application code, this is one bug or one exposed admin endpoint away from total data loss. Scope deletes to explicit keys (`UNLINK`) or per-namespace expiry, and keep flush commands in ops/migration scripts outside the served codebase. TOKEN-AS-DATA is excluded: the quoted form only counts in COMMAND POSITION — the literal must be the first element after a `(` or `[` — and the line is dropped entirely if it looks like a string denylist (a `new Set(`/`new Map(` construction, or three consecutive quoted words), because a lint/config file that merely NAMES the forbidden command is data, not a call. That gate drops the WHOLE LINE before either arm is tried, so it also silences a direct `.flushall(`/`.flushdb(` call on a line that happens to carry the denylist shape (`new Set(await client.flushAll())`) — the "data, not a call" reading does NOT exempt the call form. This rule fired on zzop's own kind of denylist (`new Set(["keys", "flushDb", "flushAll"])`) before that gate. Residual: a two-element command array is indistinguishable from a two-element denylist, so `["FLUSHDB", "ASYNC"]` still fires (correctly, it IS a command) while a two-word denylist would too. Second residual, the FALSE-NEGATIVE side of that same gate: it reads SHAPE, not reachability, so a command set that really does get dispatched later (`const DANGEROUS = new Set(["FLUSHALL"])` whose member is handed to `sendCommand` on another line) is silenced along with the inert config tables the gate was written for — separating the two needs dataflow a line-scan matcher does not have. Exposure is small in practice: the dominant real spelling is the direct `.flushall(`/`.flushdb(` call. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a dedicated cache-reset job, or a denylist the shape gate missed) with `// flushall-in-code-ok`.

`.keys(...)` called with a string-literal argument (or a quoted `'KEYS'` command literal, e.g. `sendCommand(['KEYS', pattern])`) walks the ENTIRE keyspace and blocks the single-threaded Redis server for the duration — on a production dataset this stalls every other client. Use the SCAN cursor family instead (`scanStream`/`scan_iter`, `MATCH`+`COUNT`) or maintain an explicit index set. Same TOKEN-AS-DATA gate as its sibling `redis/flushall-in-code`: the quoted `'KEYS'` form only counts in COMMAND POSITION (first element after a `(` or `[`), and the line is dropped if it looks like a string denylist (`new Set(`/`new Map(`, or three consecutive quoted words) — a config file that merely names the command is data, not a call. That denylist gate drops the WHOLE LINE before either arm is tried, so it also silences a direct `.keys('...')` call on a line that happens to carry the denylist shape (`new Set(await client.keys("user:*"))`) — the "data, not a call" reading does NOT exempt the call form. It inherits the sibling's false negative as well: the gate reads SHAPE, not reachability, so a command set that IS dispatched later (`new Set(["KEYS"])` whose member reaches `sendCommand` on another line) looks exactly like an inert config table and is silenced. Suppress a vetted case (tiny fixed keyspace, offline script) with `// keys-glob-scan-ok`.

A redis client created with `createClient(...)` (node-redis v4) or `new Redis(...)`/`new Redis.Cluster(...)` (ioredis) with no `.on('error', ...)` listener anywhere in this file — node-redis/ioredis's client is an EventEmitter that emits `'error'` on every connection blip, and with no listener attached Node's default unhandled-`error`-event behavior CRASHES the process on the first one. Note the cross-file limitation: the client may be created here and the `'error'` listener attached in another module — that's exactly the case `// client-no-error-listener-ok` is for. Attach `.on('error', ...)` where the client is created (log it, and let the reconnect strategy do its job) so a connection error degrades to a cache miss instead of killing the process.

A `.set(` call appears LEXICALLY AFTER a `.get(`/`.exists(` read in the same function, alongside a lock-ish identifier — the reported line is the first `.set(` that actually follows a read, not merely one that shares the function with it, and "same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, so a read in a sibling closure does not pair. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the set writes the key the read checked, nor that both run on the same control-flow path (a `.set(` in an `else` branch still counts). That shape (check whether a lock key is free, then set it) is a classic TOCTOU race — two concurrent callers can both pass the check before either writes, and both end up believing they hold the lock. Acquire the lock atomically instead with `SET key value NX` (add `EX`/`PX` for a TTL), a `WATCH`/`MULTI` transaction, an `.eval(` Lua script, or a redlock library. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. an atomic acquire the regex can't see) with `// lock-get-then-set-ok`.

A lock is acquired with `SET key value NX` (or `setnx`) with no `EX`/`PX`/`EXAT`/`PXAT` expiry on that same call — if the holder crashes or is killed before releasing it, the key lives forever and wedges every future caller waiting on that lock. Always pair `NX` with a TTL (e.g. `SET key value NX EX 30`) so an abandoned lock self-clears instead of requiring manual intervention. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a separate `PEXPIRE` set right after) with `// lock-no-ttl-ok`.

A `.get(` read followed by a `.set(` call whose value looks like arithmetic (`n++`, `n + 1`, `n - 1`, `Number(...)`, `parseInt(...)`) both appear in the same function — a co-occurrence heuristic for a read-modify-write counter, not proof the set actually follows the read from the same key (both patterns just match somewhere in the same function span). When it genuinely is read-then-recompute-then-write, it isn't atomic: two concurrent requests can both read the same starting value and both write the same incremented result, silently losing one of the two increments under load. Use Redis's atomic `INCR`/`INCRBY`/`DECR`/`DECRBY`/`HINCRBY` instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// counter-get-set-ok`.
